claim: GroupLens is a netnews collaborative-filtering system in which news clients display predicted scores and collect ratings while Better Bit Bureaus gather and disseminate ratings.
notes: Primary 1994 CSCW paper; do not reduce the contribution to a similarity formula alone.

claim: The paper explicitly discusses Tapestry as prior work and distinguishes GroupLens by its open, cross-site architecture and aggregate queries.
notes: Avoid claiming GroupLens invented collaborative filtering.

claim: The GroupLens architecture includes news clients and Better Bit Bureaus, with BBBs exchanging ratings through special newsgroups using the existing Usenet propagation scheme.
locator: Figure 2 and Overview, p. 177; Distributing Ratings, p. 179
notes: Local and remote BBB arrangements are both described.

claim: Users rate articles from 1 to 5; a rating may optionally include the number of seconds spent reading, and a pseudonym can preserve continuity without exposing the user's posting identity.
notes: The reading-time field was collected but was not yet used by BBB prediction in this paper; see p. 179 and p. 181.

claim: BBBs batch ratings at the reading-session level and post ratings articles to a dedicated newsgroup, relying on Usenet to propagate them.
notes: The paper also discusses alternative batching policies and the administrative cost of dedicated newsgroups.

claim: The BBB predicts missing user-article scores; the original Figure 5 uses article rows and reader columns, and missing cells represent articles not examined or not rated.
notes: The article explicitly notes the paper's matrix orientation and distinguishes an unobserved score from zero.

claim: The paper's worked example computes Ken-Lee Pearson correlation as -0.8, Ken-Meg as +1, and Ken-Nan as 0 using commonly rated articles.
notes: Pairwise means and sums are computed only over the items both users rated.

claim: The Pearson-weighted deviation formula predicts Ken's score for article 6 as 4.56.
notes: The target article has ratings from Lee and Meg; Nan has no rating for article 6 and is not included in the sum.

claim: The paper reports Nan's predicted score as 3.75, but applying the displayed Figure 5 ratings and the same Pearson-weighted deviation formula yields 3.875.
notes: Nan-Lee Pearson on shared articles 1,2,4,5 is 0.6; Nan-Meg on shared articles 1,2 is 1.0; Nan's mean is 3. The paper's 3.75 is preserved as the reported value; 3.875 is a transparent independent recomputation, not a replacement.

claim: GroupLens keeps separate rating matrices for each newsgroup because users may agree on one topic and disagree on another.
notes: Topic-local preference structure is an explicit design choice in the original system.

claim: The 1994 paper mentions a four-person Minnesota pilot of an earlier version and says a larger distributed test was being prepared, not that user preference had been established in a large-scale controlled trial.
locator: Predicting Scores, p. 181; Ongoing Experimentation, pp. 183-184
notes: The paper explicitly states that the planned test was not designed to demonstrate that users preferred filtered Netnews.

claim: The 1994 paper identifies evaluation bias when users rate only items selected by an existing filter and proposes a fully rated training set for fairer algorithm comparisons.
notes: This is a selection-bias warning, not a claim that the proposed dataset was already released.

claim: The 1994 paper discusses prediction quality, user time, BBB compute/storage and network traffic as separate scale measures.
notes: The traffic table is a scenario estimate under stated assumptions, not a measured production benchmark.

claim: A later GroupLens study reports a seven-week trial with 250 users and over 20,000 news articles.
notes: This is the 1997 follow-up paper by Miller, Riedl and Konstan, not a result from the 1994 paper.

claim: Item-based collaborative filtering estimates item-item relationships and uses them to recommend items from a user's history.
locator: Sarwar et al., WWW 2001, abstract and method
notes: A later item-neighborhood family; not part of GroupLens 1994.

claim: Matrix factorization models represent users and items with latent factors and became a prominent alternative to classic neighborhood methods.
notes: A later latent-factor family; do not attribute it to GroupLens.

claim: Bayesian Personalized Ranking optimizes personalized ranking from implicit feedback rather than treating the task solely as explicit rating prediction.
locator: Rendle et al., UAI 2009, abstract and BPR-Opt
notes: A later pairwise ranking objective; not part of the 1994 GroupLens predictor.

claim: The YouTube recommendation paper describes a deep candidate-generation model and a separate deep ranking model.
notes: A later industrial deep-recommendation architecture; used only as a broad extension pointer.
